story1159:
Brer Fox had been watching Brer Rabbit for weeks, cataloguing his tricks, noting his habits, building a case file of grievances that grew thicker every day. Brer Rabbit had outwitted him at the fishing hole, humiliated him at the barn dance, and stolen the best persimmons from the tree that Brer Fox considered his own. Something had to be done.

So Brer Fox went to work. He mixed tar and turpentine with the patience of a craftsman, shaping the mixture into a doll — a small, round figure with stubby arms and a flat face. He set it in the road where Brer Rabbit was sure to pass, propped it against a fence post, and hid in the bushes to watch.

Brer Rabbit came along, swinging his arms, whistling a tune, not a care in the world. He saw the Tar-Baby sitting in the road and stopped.

"Good morning," said Brer Rabbit. "Nice day, isn't it?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

"I said, good morning," Brer Rabbit repeated, louder. "How do you do?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

Brer Rabbit frowned. He was not accustomed to being ignored. He spoke to everyone — trees, rocks, people, animals — and they all spoke back, if only to tell him to go away. But this creature simply sat there, staring with its flat tar face, and said nothing.

"What's the matter with you?" Brer Rabbit demanded. "Cat got your tongue?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

Brer Rabbit was angry now. He struck the Tar-Baby with his right paw. His paw stuck. He struck it with his left paw. That paw stuck too. He kicked it with his right foot. His foot stuck. He kicked it with his left foot. His foot stuck. He butt the Tar-Baby with his head, and his head stuck fast.

Now Brer Rabbit was trapped, pinned to the Tar-Baby by all four limbs and his head, and Brer Fox emerged from the bushes, grinning from ear to ear.

"Well, well, well," said Brer Fox. "Look what we have here."

Brer Fox was delighted. He had Brer Rabbit exactly where he wanted him, and he intended to make the most of it. He danced around Brer Rabbit, mocking him, recounting every trick Brer Rabbit had ever played, building a case for his execution with the thoroughness of a prosecutor.

But Brer Rabbit was not finished. He was never finished. Even pinned to a Tar-Baby in the middle of the road, with Brer Fox dancing around him and planning his demise, Brer Rabbit had a trick left.

"Go ahead and kill me, Brer Fox," he said. "Roast me, drown me, skin me — I don't care. Just don't throw me in that briar patch."

Brer Fox paused. A briar patch? That sounded like a fine idea.

"Please, Brer Fox, not the briar patch!" Brer Rabbit begged, his voice rising with what sounded like genuine terror. "Anything but the briar patch!"

Brer Fox grabbed Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flung him deep into the briar patch.

To Brer Fox's astonishment, Brer Rabbit appeared on a hillside, picking burrs from his fur, and shouted back: 'Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox — bred en bawn in a brier-patch!' The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home.
story1160:
After Brer Fox captured Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declared his intent to kill and eat him. This was not idle talk — Brer Fox had been planning this moment for weeks, and he had brought a rope.

But Brer Rabbit was not ready to die. He was never ready to die. He began to plead — not for his life, exactly, but for the manner of his death, because Brer Rabbit understood that the right words at the right time could change anything.

"Roast me over a slow fire," he said. "That's the worst thing you can do to me. I can't stand a slow fire."

Brer Fox considered this. A slow fire did sound like a lot of work. He'd have to gather wood, build a fire, watch it burn down to coals, and then tend it while Brer Rabbit roasted. That would take all afternoon.

"How about I drown you?" Brer Fox offered.

"Please, Brer Fox, not drowning!" Brer Rabbit cried. "I have a fear of water. I'd rather be hanged."

"Hanged?" Brer Fox considered this. Hanging required a tree with a sturdy branch, a rope, and time. It was simpler than a slow fire, but still involved effort.

"I tell you what," Brer Fox said. "I'll throw you in the briar patch."

Brer Rabbit's eyes went wide. "Not the briar patch!" he begged. "Please, Brer Fox, anything but the briar patch! Those thorns will tear me to pieces! I'll be skinned alive! Just kill me quick — roast me, drown me, hang me — but don't throw me in the briar patch!"

The more Brer Rabbit begged to avoid the briar patch, the more determined Brer Fox became to throw him there. It was, after all, the cruelest fate Brer Rabbit could imagine. Brer Fox wanted him to suffer.

Brer Fox snatched Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flung him deep into the briar patch. The thorns caught at Brer Rabbit's fur, tore at his skin, scratched and ripped and tore.

Then Brer Fox heard a sound — a voice, coming from the hillside above. He looked up and saw Brer Rabbit sitting on a rock, picking burrs from his fur, grinning.

"Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox!" Brer Rabbit called out, laughing. "Bred en bawn in a brier-patch!" The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home. He had been born there, raised there, and learned to navigate its thorns before he could walk. Brer Fox had played right into his hands.
story1161:
Brer Fox caught Brer Rabbit again — the third time that month, which was either a testament to Brer Fox's persistence or a testament to Brer Rabbit's carelessness, depending on who was telling the story. This time, Brer Fox had a knife, and he was not interested in negotiation.

"I'm going to kill you, Brer Rabbit," he said, and his voice was flat and serious, without the theatrical menace of their usual encounters. This was real.

Brer Rabbit looked at the knife. He looked at Brer Fox. He calculated the distance to the nearest cover and determined it was too far. He was, for once, genuinely trapped.

"I don't care about dying," Brer Rabbit said, and his voice was quiet, almost resigned. "I've lived a good life. But I have one request."

Brer Fox paused. He was not a cruel being — not really — and the idea of granting a last request appealed to his sense of fairness.

"What is it?" he asked.

"I want to visit my laughing place one last time," Brer Rabbit said. "It's where I go when I want to be happy. If I can see it one more time, I'll die content."

Brer Fox was suspicious. Brer Rabbit was always suspicious. But the request seemed harmless enough — a small detour, a brief stop, and then Brer Fox could get on with his dinner.

"All right," he said. "Show me."

Brer Rabbit led Brer Fox into the woods, through a thicket of huckleberry bushes, past a stand of tall pines, to a hollow tree at the edge of a clearing. The tree was old, its trunk split by lightning, its interior a dark cavity that hummed with a strange sound.

"My laughing place is inside," Brer Rabbit whispered. "Listen."

Brer Fox leaned close to the hollow and listened. He heard a buzzing — a deep, resonant hum that grew louder the closer he put his ear. Curious, he peered into the darkness.

Inside the hollow tree was a swarm of angry bees.

They poured out of the darkness in a yellow-black cloud, their wings a blur, their stingers aimed at the nearest flesh. Brer Fox screamed and ran, flailing his arms, slapping at the bees that stung his ears, his nose, his eyes. He ran through the thicket, through the huckleberry bushes, through the creek, and he did not stop running until he was half a mile away, swollen and bleeding and bewildered.

Behind him, Brer Rabbit laughed himself silly.
story1162:
A classic African American trickster tale in which Brer Rabbit, feeling thirsty, goes to the millpond to drink and sees the moon reflected in the water. The reflection was perfect — a full, golden disk floating on the surface, so bright and round that Brer Rabbit was certain it was a cheese wheel that had fallen from someone's pocket.

He reached for it. His paw broke the surface, and the cheese shattered into a thousand shimmering pieces. He waited for the water to still, and the cheese reformed — round and golden and just out of reach.

Brer Rabbit tried everything. He lay on his belly and stretched his arm as far as it would go. He climbed a tree and leaned down from a branch. He found a stick and poked at the water. Nothing worked. The cheese remained just beyond his grasp.

Then Brer Rabbit had an idea — the kind of idea that Brer Rabbit specialized in, the kind that involved someone else doing the hard work.

He went to Brer Fox. "Brer Fox," he said, "there is a treasure in the millpond. A golden treasure, so heavy it would take two of us to pull it out."

Brer Fox was interested. Brer Fox was always interested in treasure.

They went to the millpond together. Brer Rabbit tied a rope around his waist and had Brer Fox lower him into the water. As he descended, he splashed and thrashed, stirring up the mud at the bottom, turning the water brown and murky.

"I can see it!" Brer Rabbit shouted from beneath the surface. "It's beautiful! But it's slipping away!" He splashed harder, and the moon's reflection vanished entirely.

"It sank!" Brer Rabbit cried, emerging from the water covered in mud. "The treasure sank to the bottom! You have to jump in after it, Brer Fox!"

Brer Fox jumped in. He searched the murky water for the golden treasure, found nothing but mud and weeds, and emerged cold, humiliated, and empty-handed.

Brer Rabbit was already gone. He had found some cheese elsewhere — real cheese, from someone's cooling shelf — and was eating it on a stump, licking his paws and smiling at the moon.
story1163:
Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Possum, and Brer Coon gathered at Brer Fox's house on a Saturday morning and decided to churn butter. They poured cream into the churn, took turns at the dash, and worked until their arms ached and the butter came — a solid, golden lump that they scooped out and placed in a bowl.

"We'll set it aside and share it later," Brer Fox said, and they all agreed, because they were friends, and friends share butter.

But Brer Rabbit was hungry. Not the ordinary kind of hungry — the kind that sits in your stomach and whispers suggestions. He waited until the others were gone, then he crept back to Brer Fox's house and ate all the butter. Every bit of it. He licked the bowl clean, wiped it on his fur, and left.

When the friends gathered again to share the butter, they found the bowl empty.

"Who ate the butter?" Brer Fox demanded.

They looked at each other. Brer Possum looked guilty — he always looked guilty, because he was a nervous creature who sweated when he was accused of anything, even when he was innocent.

Brer Rabbit pointed at Brer Possum. "It must have been him," he said. "Look at him. He's sweating."

Brer Possum was indeed sweating, but not because he had eaten the butter. He was sweating because he was terrified of being accused.

"I didn't eat it!" Brer Possum wailed.

"We'll see about that," Brer Rabbit said. "Here's what we'll do. We'll all lie down in the sun, and whoever ate the butter, the butter will melt out of them and we'll see the proof."

The others agreed. They lay down in the sun, side by side. But before they lay down, Brer Rabbit secretly smeared the butter on the spot where Brer Possum would lie.

As the sun warmed Brer Possum, the butter melted and appeared on his fur, glistening in the light.

"See!" Brer Rabbit cried. "The butter is coming out of him!"

Brer Possum was punished for Brer Rabbit's crime, while Brer Rabbit escaped blame through clever manipulation. The story explains why the possum plays dead when caught — he learned to be wary of being tricked again.
story1164:
Brer Rabbit, tired and hungry, found his way to a creek where he saw Brer Fox and Brer Wolf fishing. They sat on the bank, their lines in the water, their tails hanging in the current, watching the water with the patience of beings who had nowhere else to be.

Brer Rabbit was impressed. He had not eaten in two days, and the sight of fish — fat, silver, flipping in the shallows — made his stomach growl. But he did not ask for food. Brer Rabbit never asked for food. He took it.

He cut a willow branch, tied a string to it, and sat downstream, pretending to fish. In reality, he was eating the berries he found nearby — fat, sweet berries that grew in the brambles along the bank. He ate until his belly was round and his fur was stained purple.

When Brer Fox and Brer Wolf looked over and saw Brer Rabbit with a full belly, they were confused.

"How are you catching so many fish?" Brer Fox asked.

"It's my technique," Brer Rabbit said, waving his willow rod. "The best fishing is done with a snare around one's tail. You tie your tail to a root on the bank, and the current brings the fish to you."

Brer Fox and Brer Wolf looked at each other. It sounded strange, but Brer Rabbit had a full belly and they did not.

They tied their tails to a root on the bank and cast them into the current. They sat and waited. A large fish tugged at Brer Wolf's tail. He pulled. Brer Fox pulled. Their tails tangled, and the fish got away.

Brer Rabbit was already gone, well-fed and amused at their gullibility.
story1165:
Brer Rabbit, seeking to prove his superiority over Brer Fox, convinced Miss Meadows and the girls that he could ride Brer Fox like a horse. This was, by any reasonable measure, an absurd claim. Brer Fox was a predator, and Brer Rabbit was prey, and the relationship between them did not include riding.

But Brer Rabbit was persuasive. He spoke with the confidence of someone who had never let the truth stand in the way of a good story, and Miss Meadows and the girls were charmed by his audacity.

Brer Fox overheard this boast and vowed revenge. The next day, Brer Rabbit pretended to be sick and asked Brer Fox to carry him to Miss Meadows's house. "I'm too weak to walk," he moaned. "If you carry me there, I'll owe you a favor."

Brer Fox agreed, thinking he would have his revenge when they arrived. But once on Brer Fox's back, Brer Rabbit dug in his heels and rode straight to the gathering, where he showed off by declaring: "This is the way I ride Brer Fox!"

Humiliated, Brer Fox shook him off, but Brer Rabbit escaped into a hollow tree. Brer Fox enlisted Brer Wolf to help dig him out, but Brer Rabbit tricked them by claiming enemies were approaching and sent them fleeing.

The tale is part of a cycle of African trickster stories also found in the Caribbean and South America, where the rabbit trickster rides the fox or the jaguar, demonstrating that wit can conquer power.
story1166:
Brer Rabbit, proud of his speed, mocked Brer Terrapin for his slow, plodding pace. "You move like a rock rolling uphill," Brer Rabbit said. "If you were any slower, you'd be standing still."

Brer Terrapin was patient. He had been mocked before, and he had won before, and he knew that the race was not always to the swift.

"I challenge you to a race," Brer Terrapin said. "Ten miles. Winner takes the prize."

Brer Rabbit laughed. A race against a terrapin? This would be the easiest victory of his life.

But Brer Terrapin was clever. He station his wife and several family members at intervals along the race course — one at each mile marker. The plan was simple: Brer Rabbit would run ahead, reach a mile marker, and hear a voice calling out.

The race began. Brer Rabbit shot off the line like an arrow, leaving Brer Terrapin far behind. At the first mile marker, he called out: "Brer Terrapin!"

"Here I am!" a voice answered from the broomgrass.

Brer Rabbit ran faster. At the second mile marker: "Brer Terrapin!"

"Here I am!"

At the third, the fourth, the fifth — Brer Terrapin was always just ahead, always just out of reach. Brer Rabbit ran until his legs trembled and his lungs burned, but he could not shake the terrapin.

By the ninth mile, Brer Rabbit was exhausted. He stumbled, he panted, he questioned his sanity. How could a terrapin be ahead of him? He was the fastest creature in the forest!

At the finish line, Brer Terrapin was already there, sitting on a rock, waiting.

Brer Rabbit collapsed from exhaustion. The terrapin had won, and Brer Rabbit learned a lesson that speed alone does not win — strategy, family, and preparation are just as important as raw ability.
story1167:
Brer Fox, having not eaten for days, spotted a large bullfrog at the edge of the pond. The frog sat on a lily pad, its throat pulsing with each croak, its eyes half-closed in what Brer Fox interpreted as mockery.

He made a grab for the frog, but the bullfrog dove deep into the water and was gone. Brer Fox stood at the edge of the pond, dripping with mud and frustration, and made a decision that would define his day: he would drink the pond dry.

He knelt at the water's edge and began to drink. He drank and drank and drank, his belly swelling, his throat working, the water level barely dropping. The bullfrog surfaced at a safe distance and watched.

"You'll never drink it all," the bullfrog said. "The pond is deep, and your belly is small."

Brer Fox ignored him and kept drinking. His belly grew enormous — round as a watermelon, taut as a drum — but the pond level had dropped only an inch.

Other animals passed by. Brer Rabbit stopped, watched, and laughed. "What are you doing, Brer Fox?"

"I'm drinking the pond."

"Why?"

"To catch the bullfrog."

Brer Rabbit laughed so hard he fell over. The bullfrog surfaced again and offered Brer Fox advice: "Tie a stone to your neck and sink yourself. Then you can catch all the frogs underwater."

Brer Fox, not realizing he was being mocked, considered this seriously. But before he could act on it, his belly burst from the pressure, and the water rushed back in, and Brer Fox lay on the bank, wet and humiliated, while the frogs continued their chorus of croaking laughter.
story1168:
Brer Rabbit, hungry and with nothing to eat, approached Miss Cow and asked her for some milk. "My children are starving," he said. "They haven't eaten in two days. Surely you can spare a little milk."

Miss Cow looked at him with the weary patience of someone who had heard Brer Rabbit's stories before. "The milk is for my calf," she said. "I have nothing for you."

Brer Rabbit tried again. "Come to Miss Meadows's house. There is plenty of grass there, and she will share."

Miss Cow refused. She turned back to her grazing and ignored him.

Brer Rabbit left, but he did not go far. He hid behind a bush and called out in a deep, rumbling voice: "I am a wild animal, and I am going to eat you, Miss Cow!"

Miss Cow panicked. She had never heard a wild animal in the woods — she was a cow, after all, and wild animals were not something she had experience with. She ran to Miss Meadows's gate, where Brer Rabbit was waiting.

"Don't be afraid, Miss Cow," he said. "I will protect you. Just give me some milk as a thank-you."

Miss Cow, grateful and shaken, gave him all the milk he wanted.

The next day, Brer Rabbit repeated the trick with variations, eventually milking Miss Cow dry. When Miss Cow realized she had been tricked, Brer Rabbit was long gone, his children well-fed, and Miss Cow standing in the field with nothing but memories and an empty udder.
story1169:
In this pourquoi tale explaining why rabbits have short tails, Brer Rabbit once had a long, beautiful, bushy tail that he showed off constantly. It was magnificent — thick and soft, with a curl at the end that caught the light. Brer Rabbit spent hours grooming it, combing it with his paws, admiring it in the reflection of the creek.

Brer Fox grew tired of Brer Rabbit's vanity. Every conversation turned to the tail. "Have you seen my tail?" Brer Rabbit would ask. "Isn't it beautiful? I think it's the most beautiful tail in the forest."

During a cold winter, Brer Fox went ice fishing on the frozen creek. He chopped a hole in the ice, dropped his line, and caught a string of fish. When Brer Rabbit came along and saw the fish, his vanity was eclipsed by hunger.

"How did you catch those?" he asked.

"It's easy," Brer Fox said. "Cut a hole in the ice, dip your beautiful tail in, and sit there until the fish bite. Then pull up your tail with a mighty jerk, and you'll have all the fish you want."

Brer Rabbit cut a hole in the ice and dipped his beautiful tail into the water. The cold was intense, but he sat there, patient for once in his life, waiting for the fish to bite. He sat all day, and all night, and by morning his tail had frozen solid in the ice.

When evening came and Brer Rabbit was ready to leave, he gave a mighty jerk. His tail snapped off clean, leaving only the short stub that rabbits have to this day.

Brer Fox laughed heartily at the vanity that cost Brer Rabbit his finest feature. And from that day forward, Brer Rabbit never boasted about his tail again.
story1170:
Brer Rabbit, overconfident after countless successful tricks, encountered a creature he could not outsmart. It happened like this:

Brer Rabbit was walking through the forest when he met Old Man Tarrypin — the terrapin — sitting on a log, sunning himself. Brer Rabbit, feeling particularly clever that day, decided to play a trick on the old creature.

"Good morning, Old Man Tarrypin," he said. "Nice weather we're having."

"It is," the terrapin agreed.

"I suppose you're too slow to go anywhere in this nice weather," Brer Rabbit said.

"I go where I need to go," the terrapin said.

Brer Rabbit tried every trick in his repertoire. He tried false friendliness: "I'll carry you on my back, Old Man. You'll see the world." The terrapin declined. He tried reverse psychology: "I bet you're too scared to race me." The terrapin was not scared. He tried flattery: "Your shell is the most beautiful shell I've ever seen." The terrapin said thank you and went back to sunning himself.

Brer Rabbit tried fear: "There's a hawk overhead!" The terrapin pulled into his shell and waited. The hawk, if there was one, passed by.

Nothing worked. The terrapin remained calm, saw through every deception, and sat on his log like a rock — immovable, unshakable, unimpressed.

Finally, Brer Rabbit sat down beside the terrapin and admitted defeat. "I can't trick you," he said.

"No," the terrapin agreed. "You can't."

This tale serves as a caution that even the most cunning trickster may eventually meet his match, reminding listeners that overconfidence is the trickster's own greatest vulnerability.
story1171:
John Henry was born with a hammer in his hand — that's what the old people said, and the old people knew things. His mama looked at him when he came into the world, red and squalling and gripping her finger with a strength that made her gasp, and she said, "That boy is going to swing a hammer."

He grew up fast and strong, the kind of strong that doesn't come from working out but from working — from swinging a nine-pound hammer from dawn to dusk, driving steel drills into the rock face of mountains so that the railroad tunnels could be cut through. He was a steel-driving man, and he was the best that ever lived.

The hammer rang against the steel drill like a bell — a steady, rhythmic clang that echoed through the mountains, that workers could hear from three tunnels away. John Henry's rhythm was perfect. His swing was true. The drill went deeper with every stroke, and the tunnel grew longer by inches and feet, and John Henry never stopped, never slowed, never missed.

Then the steam drill came.

A salesman brought it to the worksite — a machine of iron and fire that hissed steam and spat smoke and could drill through rock faster than any man. The captain of the crew proposed a contest: man against machine. John Henry accepted. He had to. Not for pride — though he had plenty of that — but for the men who worked beside him, the men whose jobs the machine would replace.

With his shaker — a young boy who held the drill steady while John Henry swung — John Henry went to work. The hammer rang. The steam drill hissed. The rock flew. For hours the contest raged, the rhythmic ring of John Henry's hammer against the drill echoing through the mountain while the steam drill sputtered and clanked.

When the contest ended, John Henry had drilled fourteen feet while the steam drill had managed only nine. He had beaten the machine.
story1172:
After defeating the steam drill, John Henry's heart gave out. It was a simple as that — the organ that had pumped blood through his massive body for thirty years, the heart that had driven the hammer through fourteen feet of solid rock, simply stopped. It had been asked to do too much, and it could do no more.

With his hammer still in his hand, the mighty steel-driving man collapsed. His shaker — the young boy who had held the drill steady — caught him as he fell, lowering him gently to the ground. The other workers gathered around as the man who had beaten the machine lay still.

They called for water. They fanned him with their hats. They whispered his name. But John Henry was gone.

His woman — Polly Ann in some versions, Mary Ann in others, Julia Ann in still others — took up his hammer after his death. She was not as strong as John Henry, but she was determined, and she drove steel into the rock with a fury that silenced the men who had doubted her. She finished the tunnel that John Henry had started, and she raised their children alone.

John Henry's funeral was a massive gathering. Workers came from every railroad line — from Virginia to Alabama, from the mountains to the coast — to pay their respects. They brought hammers and laid them at his grave. They sang the ballad that had already begun to form around his death:

"John Henry said to his shaker,
'You know I'm gonna die.
You go home and tell my Polly Ann
Not to grieve after me.'"

The ballad spread rapidly across the South, carried by itinerant workers, becoming one of the most recorded folk songs in American history. More than just a story, John Henry's death became a symbol of the human cost of industrialization and the struggle of Black workers against the dehumanizing forces of progress that sought to replace them.
story1173:
High John the Conqueror was born an African prince, and he lived like one — with pride, with fire, with the unshakable knowledge that the world belonged to him. But the slave ships came, as they always came, and High John was captured and sold into slavery, transported across the ocean in a hold so dark and cramped that he could not stand, could not turn, could not see the face of the man chained beside him.

But High John's spirit could not be captured. It could not be chained, could not be sold, could not be broken. In America, he became a trickster — a figure of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved, his power disguised as mischief, his rebellion disguised as humor.

He fell in love with the Devil's beautiful daughter, and the Devil, enraged, set John a series of impossible tasks. John must clear sixty acres of forest in half a day. He must plow the land, plant it with corn, and harvest it all before sunset.

The Devil's daughter, who loved John truly, secretly gave him a magical axe that felled trees on its own and a magical plow that turned the soil without effort. John completed every task with time to spare.

The Devil then tried to kill John by setting his bed on fire. But John escaped by shape-shifting — he became a puddle of water on the floor, then a fly on the wall, then a bolt of lightning that shot through the window and disappeared into the sky.

John and the Devil's daughter stole the Devil's swiftest horses and fled. The Devil pursued them, but John and his lover transformed themselves into various forms — a pond and a duck, a church and a preacher — evading capture at every turn until they escaped forever.

According to the lore collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John's power was not just personal but communal. When the whip fell, John would 'take the spirit of his people out of their bodies' so they could not feel the pain. He could be heard laughing in the slave quarters at night, a sound that reminded the enslaved that freedom was coming. He planted the idea of emancipation in the minds of white people and provoked the Civil War itself.
story1174:
According to the lore collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John the Conqueror was more than a trickster — he was a spirit of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved. Born an African prince, John was captured and sold into slavery, but his spirit could never be broken.

When the whip fell, John would 'take the spirit of their people out of their bodies' so they could not feel the pain. He could be heard laughing in the slave quarters at night, a sound that reminded the enslaved that freedom was coming. The old people said that when you heard John laughing, you knew that the world was about to change.

John planted the idea of emancipation in the minds of white people and provoked the Civil War itself. He whispered in the ears of abolitionists, steeled the nerves of conductors on the Underground Railroad, and gave courage to the soldiers who fought for freedom. He was everywhere and nowhere, a presence felt but never seen.

After emancipation, John returned to Africa. But he left his power here. "He waits to return when his people call him," Hurston wrote. And his people have called him — in the civil rights movement, in the struggles for justice, in every moment when Black Americans have needed the strength to resist, to endure, to prevail.

High John's root — a dried tuber carried in a mojo bag — remains a central talisman in Hoodoo practice, symbolizing unbreakable spirit and the certainty of victory over oppression. The root is small, brown, unremarkable in appearance, but those who carry it say it burns with the warmth of High John's spirit — a warmth that never fades, a fire that never goes out.

To carry High John's root is to carry the memory of a prince who was enslaved but never conquered, who lost his freedom but never lost his fire, and who left behind a power that anyone — man, woman, or child — can tap into if they are willing to believe that the world can be changed.
story1175:
In May 1803, a group of seventy-five Igbo people from what is now Nigeria were captured and transported to Georgia. They were chained together in the hold of a ship called the York, and they survived the Middle Passage — that horrors of that crossing are a story in themselves — and they arrived in Savannah alive, which was more than many could say.

They were loaded onto a small vessel at Savannah and shipped to St. Simons Island to be sold at the slave market. The Igbo were high-ranking warriors among their people, and they were not the kind of men who accepted bondage. They had been captured through trickery, through the treachery of rival tribes who sold them to the Europeans, and they had no intention of remaining slaves.

On the small vessel, chained together, guarded by a handful of white slavers, the Igbo made their decision. They rose up against their captors. They fought with chains, with fists, with the fury of men who had nothing left to lose. They took control of the ship and forced it aground at Dunbar Creek.

There, in a coordinated act of mass resistance, they walked deliberately into the water.

They walked in chains, still chained together, still singing in their native Igbo language. The water rose around their ankles, their knees, their waists. The slavers on the shore screamed at them to stop, to come back, to submit. The Igbo did not stop. They walked until the water closed over their heads, and they drowned together, bound by chains in life and in death.

Some oral accounts say they did not drown at all but transformed into buzzards and flew back across the Atlantic to Africa. The buzzards circled over Dunbar Creek, their wings casting shadows on the water, and then they flew east, over the ocean, over the horizon, back to the land they had been stolen from.

The site, Igbo Landing, became sacred ground in African American memory, birthing the enduring 'Flying Africans' mythos — the belief that those who refused to be enslaved could literally fly home to freedom. The Igbo did not die. They rose.
story1176:
In this beloved African American folktale collected by Virginia Hamilton, enslaved Africans secretly retained the magical ability to fly — a power brought from their homeland, carried in their bones, in their blood, in the songs they sang in the fields.

One day, as an old man named Toby worked in the cotton fields under a cruel overseer's lash, he began to whisper ancient words in a language the other slaves had forgotten. The words were old — older than the fields, older than the chains, older than the ocean that had brought them here. They were words of power, words of flight, words that unlocked the magic that every enslaved person carried but could not access.

One by one, the enslaved people remembered. Sarah, carrying her baby on her back, rose into the air. She rose slowly at first, testing her weight, finding her balance, and then she rose faster, her feet leaving the ground, her body lifting like a bird taking flight. Young Jesse and his mother lifted off next, their arms spread wide, their faces full of wonder.

The overseer watched in disbelief as worker after worker soared into the sky. He ran toward them, shouting, swinging his whip, but the whip could not reach them — they were above him now, above the fields, above the chains, above the world that had tried to hold them down.

Toby himself flew last, calling the magic words until all who remembered were gone. He rose into the air with a grace that belied his age, and he followed the others across the sky, across the ocean, back to Africa.

But some chose to stay. Their wings were clipped by the harshness of bondage, their magic worn thin by years of cruelty. They watched their brothers and sisters disappear into the clouds and returned to the fields, to the chains, to the life they could not leave. And their descendants tell the story still — the story of the people who could fly, who did fly, who flew home to freedom.
story1177:
A Gullah version of the Flying Africans legend, recorded by the Federal Writers' Project in the late 1930s. Wallace Quarterman, a Gullah man born in 1844 on Sapelo Island, Georgia, recounted that the Igbo people who drowned at Dunbar Creek did not die at all.

According to the oral tradition passed down through generations, the Igbo 'rise out of the water and turn into buzzards and fly back to Africa.' In Gullah belief, the buzzard is not a carrion eater but a sacred bird that carries the souls of the dead back across the Atlantic. The buzzard circles over the water three times, then rises into the sky and flies east, carrying the souls of the Igbo on its wings.

This story reflects the deep spiritual connection between the Gullah people and their West African ancestors, and the belief that death by water was not an end but a transformation. The water that separated Africa from America was the same water that could carry the dead home. You went into the water a slave, and you came out of the water a free soul, flying east, flying home.

The buzzard's circling flight over the Georgia coast is seen as the lingering presence of those who refused to be slaves, forever watching and waiting. The Gullah say that if you see a buzzard circling over Dunbar Creek at dawn, it is carrying another soul home.

Wallace Quarterman spoke of this with the certainty of a man who had seen it — or whose grandparents had seen it, or whose great-grandparents had told them. The story was not metaphor to him. It was history. It was truth. The Igbo flew, and their descendants — the Gullah, the Geechee, the people of the Sea Islands — carried that truth in their bones.
story1178:
On Christmas night, 1895, in a St. Louis saloon, the notorious bad-man Stagolee shot William 'Billy' Lyons after a dispute. In the folk tradition, the argument began when Billy Lyons snatched Stagolee's prized Stetson hat from his head and refused to return it.

Stagolee warned him: 'I don't care what you do with me, but don't you mess with my Stetson hat.' The hat was not just a hat. It was a symbol — of status, of style, of the particular brand of defiance that Stagolee carried like a second skin. To touch the hat was to touch the man, and to touch the man was to invite the consequences.

Billy laughed and refused. Stagolee drew his .44 pistol. Billy begged for his life, pleading that he had a wife and children, but Stagolee replied, 'I don't care about your wife and kids — you should have thought of them before you touched my Stetson hat.' He shot Billy dead.

The song spread like wildfire across America, with each new version making Stagolee more mythic. In some versions, Stagolee was a plantation slave who killed his master. In others, he was a railroad worker. In still others, he was a cowboy, a gambler, a man who lived outside the law.

The hat remained central. It was the catalyst, the symbol, the thing that mattered more than life itself. In a world where Black men were expected to submit — to bow their heads, to step aside, to accept their place — Stagolee refused. He wore his hat at an angle that dared the world to challenge him, and when Billy Lyons did, Stagolee responded with the only language that the world of power understood: violence.

The song transformed a common barroom murder into a foundational American outlaw legend — the quintessential 'bad man' who answered to no man and no law.
story1179:
After Stagolee was hanged for murder, he arrived at the gates of Hell, still wearing his Stetson hat and carrying his .44 pistol. The Devil was waiting for him — he had heard about Stagolee, had heard about the murder, had heard about the defiance — and he was ready to claim his soul.

But Stagolee was not the kind of man who submitted to anyone, not even the Devil.

"Welcome to Hell," the Devil said. "You'll spend eternity burning for your sins."

Stagolee looked at the Devil. He looked at the flames. He looked at his pistol.

"I don't think so," he said.

He pulled his pistol and challenged the Devil himself. The Devil, for all his power, found he could not control Stagolee. The flames that burned others only made Stagolee warmer. The chains that bound others broke in his hands. The torments that drove others mad only made Stagolee angrier.

Stagolee kicked the Devil off his throne, sat down on it himself, and took over the running of Hell. In some versions, he set all the lost souls free, opening the gates and letting them walk out into the light. In others, he ran Hell more efficiently than the Devil ever did — organizing the damned, assigning punishments, maintaining order with the same iron will that had made him the baddest man on earth.

The Devil eventually begged God to let Stagolee into Heaven, if only to get rid of him. But Heaven refused as well — Stagolee had too much blood on his hands, too many sins on his ledger, too much defiance in his soul.

So Stagolee remained master of his own domain, sitting on the Devil's throne in Hell, wearing his Stetson hat, carrying his .44 pistol, answering to absolutely no one. This tale of a man so bad that Hell itself could not hold him became a cornerstone of African American 'toasts' — narrative poems celebrating the ultimate rebellious figure who fears neither God nor Devil.
story1180:
The folk ballad describes Stagolee's funeral as an event unlike any before seen. Thousands of people came from miles around to see the baddest man who ever lived laid to rest. A procession of mourners stretched for blocks — the women weeping, the men silent and respectful, the children peeking from behind their mothers' skirts.

His coffin was reportedly so fine it cost more than most men earned in a year. It was polished mahogany, lined with satin, fitted with brass handles that gleamed in the sunlight. The ballad describes the funeral train, the flowers, the hymns sung over his grave.

Yet even in death, Stagolee remained defiant. The women who heard of his death 'could not stay at home,' rushing to the funeral in droves. They came to see the man they had heard about in songs and stories, the man who had stood up to the law, to the Devil, to the world itself.

Verses describe how 'the women in the West' heard the news and lamented, cementing Stagolee's status as a tragic romantic figure — a man whose very name was enough to make women weep and men tremble.

Stagolee's funeral became a set-piece in African American folk memory: the moment when the community paused to honor a man who, for all his violence, represented a kind of freedom — the freedom to be utterly oneself, without apology or compromise, in a world that demanded constant submission from Black men. Stagolee wore his hat at an angle. He carried his pistol openly. He answered to no one. And when he died, the people honored him not because he was good, but because he was free.
story1181:
Jack, a lazy mountain boy, decided to seek his fortune after his mother grew tired of his idleness. "Get out of this house," she said, "and don't come back until you've made something of yourself." Jack kissed her on the cheek, picked up a stick, and walked into the world.

He arrived at a king's house and learned that giants had overrun the king's 'newground' — newly cleared land that the king intended to farm — and would not let anyone work it. Anyone who went against them was eaten. The king's men had tried. They had not returned.

Jack volunteered. He was not brave — Jack was the opposite of brave — but he was hungry, and the king had promised a reward, and Jack figured that if he couldn't outfight the giants, he could at least outtalk them.

He encountered the giants in the newground, and rather than fighting them directly, he used cleverness to turn them against one another. He told the first giant that the second had insulted his wife. He told the second giant that the third had stolen his tools. He told the third giant that the first was planning to take his land.

The giants fought among themselves. They swung their clubs and threw their rocks and roared with fury, and when the dust settled, the giants were either dead or fled, and Jack claimed the reward.

This tale originates from the European Jack Tale tradition but was carried into Appalachia by Scots-Irish settlers and preserved, particularly within African American communities of the Southern mountains, where Jack became a symbol of the clever underdog who overcomes overwhelming odds through wit rather than strength. In Affrilachian versions, Jack's voice and humor are distinctly rooted in African American storytelling cadences, and his trickery carries the additional weight of a people who had to outwit their oppressors daily.
story1182:
The Appalachian African American version of the classic Jack and the Beanstalk tale. Jack, a poor mountain boy, traded his family's only cow for a handful of seemingly worthless beans. His mother, furious, threw the beans out the window.

Overnight, a giant beanstalk grew all the way to the sky. It erupted from the ground with a sound like thunder, its trunk thick as a barrel, its leaves spreading across the heavens like a green canopy. Jack climbed it.

He climbed for hours, his hands blistered, his legs trembling, until he broke through the clouds and found himself in a world above the clouds — a giant's castle, its walls made of stone, its chimneys belching smoke that smelled of roasting meat.

He met the giant's wife, who was kind and afraid. "My husband smells the blood of a Christian," she whispered. "He'll eat you if he finds you."

She hid Jack in a cupboard, and the giant came in, roaring and stomping, his footsteps shaking the floor. "Fee-fi-fo-fum!" he bellowed. "I smell the blood of a Christian!"

"It's just the bones from last night's dinner," the giant's wife said, and the giant sat down to eat.

Jack stole the giant's gold. He stole the hen that laid golden eggs. He stole the magical singing harp. And when the giant pursued him down the beanstalk, Jack chopped it down with an axe, and the giant fell to his death.

In the Appalachian versions, the setting shifts to mountain terrain, and Jack's language reflects the regional dialect. African American tellers of the tale emphasized themes of economic survival and outwitting a powerful, deadly enemy — resonant with a community navigating a world where power was concentrated in hostile hands.
story1183:
Jack left home seeking adventure and met a group of robbers in the forest. Rather than fleeing — as any sensible person would — Jack cleverly ingratiated himself with them, pretending to be a fierce outlaw. He boasted of crimes he had never committed, described escapes he had never made, and name-dropped gangs that did not exist.

The robbers were impressed. They took him into their band.

They planned a raid on a wealthy house. When the robbers sent Jack in to check if the house was empty, Jack found it full of people — a family of twelve, plus servants — but he convinced the robbers the house was safe by using ventriloquism and mimicry, speaking in different voices from different windows to make it sound like the house was empty.

During the robbery attempt, Jack deliberately made noise to alert the householders, then blamed the commotion on ghosts. The robbers fled in terror, leaving all the loot behind.

Jack collected the abandoned treasure and returned home a rich man.

The tale highlights Jack's hallmark traits: he is not particularly brave or strong, but he is quick-witted and lucky, always landing on his feet through a combination of clever words and fortunate circumstances. In Affrilachian versions, Jack's voice and humor are distinctly rooted in African American storytelling cadences.
story1184:
Jack was tasked with spending a night alone in a haunted cabin in the woods as a test of courage. The cabin was supposedly infested with 'varmints' — supernatural creatures that had driven away everyone who came before. No one had survived a night in the cabin. No one had lasted until dawn.

Jack, being too lazy and stubborn to be properly scared, settled into the cabin for the night. He found a rocking chair by the fire, a jug of something warm on the shelf, and a blanket on the bed. He rocked, he drank, he waited.

As midnight approached, he heard scratching at the door. Howling from the chimney. Strange shapes moving in the shadows. The temperature dropped. The fire flickered.

Rather than fleeing, Jack banged pots, shouted insults, and threw things at the darkness. He threw a boot at the scratching sound and heard a yelp. He poured water down the chimney and heard a splash. He sang at the top of his lungs — off-key, loud, and profane — and the shadows retreated.

His sheer orneriness and refusal to be intimidated somehow drove the varmints away. By morning, the cabin was peaceful, and Jack collected the reward.

In some versions, the varmints are revealed to be pranksters in costume — neighbors who wanted to scare Jack away for their own amusement. In others, they are genuine supernatural beings defeated by Jack's audacious spirit. The story resonates in the African American Appalachian tradition as a tale of facing one's fears with humor and determination rather than weapons.
story1185:
In Gullah Geechee folklore, a young man named Emmet Fisher fell in love with a beautiful but mysterious woman who lived deep in the marsh. She appeared one evening at the edge of the water, her hair black as the night, her eyes dark and deep, her voice like honey over gravel. She said her name was nothing that he could pronounce, and she smiled in a way that made him forget his own.

Against all warnings — his grandmother told him not to go near the marsh, his mother told him to find a girl from the village, his friends told him there was something wrong about a woman who lived alone in the swamp — Emmet married her.

They lived together in his house, and for a time, everything was fine. She cooked for him, cleaned for him, lay beside him at night. But there was something wrong. She never ate in front of him. She never undressed in his presence. She left every night after he fell asleep and returned before dawn, smelling of marsh water and something else — something metallic, like blood.

One night, Emmet pretended to be asleep. He lay still, his eyes barely open, and watched his bride remove her skin. She peeled it off like a garment — first the arms, then the torso, then the legs — and hung it on a hook behind the door. Beneath the skin was a creature that was not human: a skinless red thing with bat-like wings and fingers that ended in claws.

She flew out through the keyhole to ride her victims — sitting on their chests and stealing their breath while they slept.

Emmet confronted her the next morning, but she denied everything. He sprinkled cayenne pepper and salt around the room, and when she shed her skin again that night, she could not put it back on — the pepper burned her raw flesh. She fled into the night, forever skinless.

The Boo Hag legend explains why Gullah people paint their doors and windows 'haint blue,' hang brooms by the entrance, and keep salt and pepper mixtures in their corners — all ways to confuse, repel, or trap these night-visiting entities that drain the life force of the living.
story1186:
The Plat-Eye is a malevolent, shapeshifting spirit in Gullah Geechee folklore, believed to be the restless ghost of a person who was wronged in life and died with unfinished business. The spirit cannot rest. It cannot move on. It is trapped between the living world and the dead, bound to the place where it died by the injustice that killed it.

The Plat-Eye takes various forms — an animal with one large glowing eye, a ball of light, or a shadowy figure — and haunts the place of its death or burial. It is intensely territorial and will attack anyone who intrudes upon its domain.

Unlike the Boo Hag, which enters homes, the Plat-Eye stays outdoors, lurking in swamps, crossroads, and graveyards. It appears at dusk, when the light is failing and the shadows are long, and it glows — a single, pulsing light in the darkness, like a lantern carried by something that has no body.

To ward off a Plat-Eye, Gullah people carry a small burlap sachet filled with equal parts gunpowder and sulfur, whose strong smell offends the spirit and drives it away. The sachet must be carried at all times when traveling near the Plat-Eye's territory, and it must be renewed every new moon, when the spirit's power is at its weakest.

The Plat-Eye tradition reflects African beliefs in ancestral spirits who require proper burial rites to find peace, combined with the harsh reality of the many enslaved people who died unjustly and were buried in unmarked graves along the Sea Islands coast. The Plat-Eyes are the ghosts of those who were murdered, who were buried without ceremony, who were denied the rituals that would have set their spirits free. They wander because no one remembers their names. They haunt because no one marked their graves. They glow in the darkness because they want to be seen — they want someone to know they were here.
story1187:
Jacky-My-Lantern is a wandering spirit who carries a flickering light through the swamps at night, luring travelers from the safety of the road into the treacherous marshland. According to Uncle Remus, Jacky-My-Lantern was once a man who made a deal with the Devil and was cursed to wander the earth with only a lantern made from a hollowed turnip and a coal of fire to light his way, never finding rest.

The deal was simple: the man would give the Devil his soul in exchange for riches. The Devil agreed, and the man received his riches — gold, silver, fine clothes, a big house. But when the time came to pay, the man reneged. He refused to hand over his soul. He thought he had outwitted the Devil.

The Devil does not like being outwitted. He appeared to the man one night and took everything — the gold, the silver, the clothes, the house — and then he cursed the man to wander the earth with nothing but a lantern made from a turnip and a coal of fire, never finding rest, never finding home.

When travelers see the bobbing light in the swamp and follow it, hoping to reach shelter, they soon find themselves sinking into the bog, unable to find their way back. The light leads them deeper and deeper into the marsh, and by the time they realize their mistake, they are lost.

The only protection against Jacky-My-Lantern is to carry a Bible, wear your coat inside out, or avoid being out at night near the swamp. The legend blends African American folklore with European jack-o'-lantern traditions, creating a distinctively Southern cautionary tale about the dangers of the unknown and the consequences of making deals with dark forces.
story1188:
The Bell Witch of Tennessee is one of America's most famous supernatural legends, and its African American dimensions are often overlooked. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation near Adams, Tennessee, had their own interpretations of the entity that tormented the Bell family from 1817 to 1821.

While white accounts describe the witch as the ghost of Kate Batts, a neighbor who bore a grudge against John Bell, African American oral traditions viewed the Bell Witch as a 'haint' connected to the horrors of slavery itself — a spirit born from the suffering of the enslaved on the plantation. The entity that tormented the Bell family was, in the African American understanding, a manifestation of the violence that permeated the plantation system.

Some accounts from formerly enslaved people describe the witch as a Boo Hag-like entity that could shed its skin and fly, visiting the slave quarters at night and tormenting those who had nowhere to escape. The enslaved community used their own protective measures — salt, sulfur, haint blue paint, and conjure bags — to ward off the entity, often with greater success than the Bells' reliance on prayer and Christian ritual.

The Bell Witch thus represents a convergence of African and European supernatural traditions on American soil. The ghost that haunted the Bell family was not just the spirit of Kate Batts; it was the accumulated grief, rage, and suffering of every enslaved person who had lived and died on that land. It was the plantation's own conscience, manifesting as a force that could not be prayed away.
story1189:
Collected by Joel Chandler Harris in the Uncle Remus stories, 'A Plantation Witch' tells of supernatural occurrences on the plantation. Uncle Remus recounts that witches on the plantation could transform into animals, particularly haunts and hags that rode people at night.

According to the tale, a young enslaved man named Toby was ridden by a hag every night and would wake up exhausted, as if he had been running all night. His body ached. His clothes were dirty. His feet were sore. But he had no memory of what happened after he fell asleep.

An old conjure woman told him to sprinkle salt and pepper around his bed before sleeping. She showed him how to make a line of salt across the doorway and how to place a bundle of herbs under his pillow.

When the hag came that night, she could not approach him. The salt burned her feet. The pepper made her eyes water. She could not enter the room, and she could not ride him, and she was furious.

In a rage, she revealed herself as a woman from the neighboring plantation who had been jealous of Toby's good fortune. She had been using dark magic to torment him, stealing his strength while he slept.

She promised to leave Toby alone if he never revealed her secret. Toby agreed, and the hag never troubled him again.

But from that night on, Toby kept a container of salt and a Bible under his pillow, just in case. The tale illustrates the deeply held African American folk belief in night-hags and the practical, protective measures used against them — measures that drew on African spiritual traditions and adapted them to the conditions of slavery.
story1190:
A young Gullah man named Joshua fell in love with a woman named Eloise, the most beautiful woman on the Sea Islands. She had eyes like the ocean at dawn and a voice like the tide, and Joshua was lost from the moment he saw her.

They were to be married on a Saturday evening, at the water's edge, where the live oaks hung their moss over the sand and the tide came in soft and slow. But on the night before the wedding, Eloise fell ill and died of a sudden fever. She was twenty years old.

Joshua was heartbroken. He stopped eating. He stopped speaking. He sat on the beach where they were to have been married and stared at the water.

On the night of what would have been their wedding, Joshua sat alone on the beach, grieving. The moon was full, the tide was high, and the waves whispered against the sand. At midnight, Eloise appeared before him, dressed in white, her eyes glowing faintly with a light that was not moonlight.

She said she had returned to claim her wedding.

Joshua, driven by love, danced with her on the moonlit shore as the waves crashed around them. They danced and danced, and Joshua forgot that she was dead, and Eloise forgot that she was a ghost, and for a few hours they were together again.

An old conjure woman saw them and rushed to intervene, throwing salt between Joshua and the ghost bride. The spirit vanished with a wail.

The conjure woman explained that the ghost bride had come to take Joshua with her to the spirit world — if he had danced until dawn, his soul would have been hers forever. Joshua painted his door 'haint blue' and never went near the beach at night again.
story1191:
On a Virginia plantation, the master hired a notorious slave driver to break the spirit of the enslaved people. The man was cruel beyond measure — he whipped without provocation, worked people until they collapsed, and took pleasure in their suffering. Whippings and punishments only increased, and the people grew desperate.

An old conjure doctor named Uncle Monday was called from a neighboring plantation. He was old — older than anyone could remember — with white hair and dark skin and eyes that saw things that were not visible to ordinary sight. He walked through the quarters, speaking to the people, gathering roots and herbs from the forest, and preparing something in a small leather pouch.

He prepared a special mojo bag and buried it at the crossroads near the plantation gate. That night, the slave driver could not sleep. He was tormented by nightmares of his victims — faces he had whipped, bodies he had broken, people he had killed. He saw them standing at the foot of his bed, silent and accusing.

The next day, he was thrown from his horse for no reason. The horse shied at a shadow that was not there, and the driver went flying, breaking his arm and cracking his ribs.

Within a week, he fled the plantation, claiming it was haunted.

The master, furious, accused Uncle Monday of witchcraft and threatened to have him whipped. Uncle Monday calmly pointed at a tree stump, and it burst into flames. The master never touched him.

Uncle Monday taught the people that conjure was their protection, passed from Africa, and that no master could ever truly break what the spirits protected. The tale embodies the power of conjure as a form of psychological and spiritual resistance against the violence of slavery.
story1192:
In Hoodoo tradition, a Jack Ball is one of the most powerful conjure objects — a small ball made from wax, graveyard dust, personal concerns of the target, and the rootworker's own blood, empowered by nine days of prayer and fasting.

The tale tells of a rootworker who created a Jack Ball for a man who had been betrayed by his lover. The woman had promised to marry him, taken his money, and run off with another man. The man was devastated — not just heartbroken but spiritually broken, unable to eat, unable to sleep, unable to think of anything but her.

The rootworker made the Jack Ball in secret, working by candlelight in a room where no one could see. She shaped the wax into a perfect sphere, mixed in the graveyard dust, added a strand of the woman's hair (which the man had kept), and pricked her finger to add a drop of her own blood. She prayed over it for nine days, fasting on bread and water, calling on the spirits of the dead to empower the object.

The Jack Ball was said to be able to 'follow' its target anywhere. It rolled by itself, knocked on doors, appeared in unexpected places. The unfaithful woman could not rest anywhere — the Jack Ball followed her from town to town, room to room, bed to bed. Her conscience tormented her. She could not sleep, could not eat, could not find peace.

In the end, she returned to make amends. The Jack Ball stopped following her only when she had repaid every cent, apologized with sincerity, and acknowledged the wrong she had done.

The making of a Jack Ball is one of the most secret and solemn rites in Hoodoo practice. Such stories reinforced the belief in the tangible power of conjure and the importance of honoring one's commitments.
story1193:
In African American conjure tradition, the crossroads is the most spiritually charged place — the intersection where the physical world meets the spirit world. At the crossroads, the veil between the living and the dead is thin, and the spirits walk among the living.

The story tells of a young man who went to a crossroads at midnight seeking power. He was instructed by a rootworker to bring a black chicken, a bottle of whiskey, and nine silver dimes. At the crossroads, he was to draw an X on the ground with a knife, light a black candle, and wait.

The spirits would test him with terrors. He would see things that were not there, hear voices that were not real, feel hands that had no bodies. He must not run. He must not scream. He must sit in the center of the X and wait.

According to some accounts, a figure would appear — sometimes the Devil, sometimes an old man, sometimes a faceless presence — and offer a deal: power and fortune in exchange for his soul.

The crossroads spirit could teach the secrets of conjure, give winning lottery numbers, or make an enemy sick. But the price was always steep. Those who succeeded at the crossroads gained power that lasted a lifetime. Those who failed lost their minds or their lives.

The crossroads story blends African spiritual traditions (where crossroads are home to the trickster god Eshu-Elegba) with the American experience of desperate people seeking power in a world that denied them any. The crossroads was the one place where the powerless could become powerful, where the weak could become strong, where the rules of the plantation did not apply.
story1194:
In Hoodoo tradition, graveyard dust is among the most potent and dangerous conjure materials. It is dust from the center of a grave — specifically, the grave of someone who had been a faithful spouse, a good provider, a person who lived well and died with their affairs in order.

The tale tells of a woman whose husband was stolen away by a rival through love magic. The rival had used a honey jar, a followed-me-boy spell, or some other conjure to bind the husband's affections, and he had left his wife and children to be with the other woman.

Desperate, the woman went to a rootworker. The rootworker instructed her to go to a graveyard at midnight, find the grave of someone who had been a faithful spouse, and collect dust from the center of the grave. She had to leave a silver dime as payment, walk backward away from the grave, and never look back.

The graveyard dust was then mixed with the husband's personal effects — a hair, a button, a piece of his clothing — and buried under the doorstep.

According to the story, the husband returned within three days, unable to explain why he could not stay away. He walked through the door and felt a warmth he had not felt in months, and he knew he was home.

The rootworker warned that graveyard dust could be used for either love or hate, healing or harm, and that using it to harm an innocent would cause the dust to 'turn' on the user. The story teaches that the dead must be treated with respect and that conjure power requires not just knowledge but moral responsibility.
story1195:
Mojo bags — small red flannel pouches filled with roots, herbs, coins, and personal objects — are central to Hoodoo practice, and their creation is surrounded by elaborate lore. One traditional story tells of a conjure woman named Aunt Polly who made mojo bags for her entire community.

People came from miles around seeking her bags for luck in love, protection from harm, success in gambling, or revenge against enemies. She made each bag by hand, selecting the ingredients with the care of a jeweler selecting stones. For love, she used lodestone, damiana, and a locks of hair from both parties. For protection, she usedJohn the Conqueror root, iron nails, and a verse from the Bible written on brown paper. For gambling, she used a rabbit's foot, a lodestone, and a silver dime.

The most famous story involves a young man about to gamble with a cruel white landowner who always cheated. Aunt Polly made him a mojo containing John the Conqueror root, a silver dime, and a petition written on brown paper. She told him to keep it in his left pocket and never let it touch the ground.

At the gambling table, the young man won every hand. The landowner, enraged, accused him of cheating, but the mojo protected him from harm — the landowner's pistol would not fire. The young man escaped with his winnings and never gambled again.

The mojo bag tradition reflects the African American belief that spiritual protection is carried with you, a portable connection to the power of the ancestors and the conjure tradition.
story1196:
In Gullah Geechee creation folklore, the frog was one of the first creatures and played a crucial role in shaping the Sea Islands. The story tells that in the beginning, there was only water everywhere — no land, no islands, no place for people to stand.

The Creator needed someone to dive to the bottom and bring up mud to make land. All the big animals tried and failed — the bear could not hold his breath long enough, the whale could not reach the bottom, the eagle could not dive deep enough. They tried and tried, and every time they surfaced empty-handed.

Finally, the little green frog volunteered. The big animals laughed at him. "You?" they said. "You are too small. You are too weak. You will never make it."

But the frog dove down, down, down, past the fish, past the whales, past the darkness, to the very bottom of the ocean. He scooped up a mouthful of mud and kicked his way back up.

When he surfaced, the Creator took the mud from the frog's mouth and formed the Sea Islands — the chain of low, marshy islands that stretches along the coast of Georgia and South Carolina. The islands grew from the mud, rising from the water like the backs of sleeping whales.

As a reward, the frog was allowed to live both in water and on land and to sing the loudest song of any creature at dawn.

This pourquoi tale explains both the origin of the Gullah homeland and why frogs sing so loudly at daybreak, connecting the Gullah people's deep sense of place with the natural world around them.
story1197:
On a rice plantation along the South Carolina coast, an old Gullah woman named Cunjah Maum was known as the most powerful rootworker in the Lowcountry. She lived alone in a cabin at the edge of the marsh, surrounded by herbs and roots and the smoke of sweet grass, and people came to her from miles around for healing, for protection, for justice.

When the master's daughter fell ill with a mysterious fever that no doctor could cure — and the plantation had its own doctor, a white man who came from Charleston once a month — the master reluctantly sent for Cunjah Maum.

She came to the big house and asked for three things: a lock of the girl's hair, water from the spring that flowed east, and privacy. The master granted all three.

Cunjah Maum ground roots and leaves into a paste, mixed it with the spring water, and sang songs in an African language over the mixture. The songs were old — older than slavery, older than the plantation, older than the ocean that separated Africa from America. They were songs of healing, songs of power, songs that called on the ancestors to intervene.

She rubbed the paste on the girl's forehead and feet and prayed to ancestors she could see standing in the corners of the room — spirits that no one else could see but that filled the room with a warmth that the master felt but could not explain.

Within three days, the girl recovered completely.

The master offered Cunjah Maum money, but she refused. She asked instead that her grandson be taught to read. The master, grateful and perhaps a little shaken by what he had witnessed, agreed.

Cunjah Maum's story embodies the Gullah belief in the power of rootwork to heal not just the body but to negotiate justice in a world where Black people had little power. Her refusal of money and demand for literacy represents the deeper value of knowledge over wealth.
story1198:
In this Gullah Geechee variant of the classic trickster race tale, Brer Cooter (the terrapin) and Brer Deer were both courting the same young lady. She was beautiful — the most beautiful woman in the village — and she declared she would marry whichever one won a ten-mile race.

Brer Deer laughed at the slow-moving terrapin. "You?" he said. "You couldn't win a race against a rock."

But Brer Cooter was clever. He knew he could not outrun Brer Deer — no terrapin could outrun a deer — but he could outthink him.

He station nine members of his family at each mile marker along the race course, and he himself waited at the finish line, right in front of the young lady's door. At nine o'clock, the race began.

Brer Deer sprang forward while Brer Cooter disappeared. At the first mile marker, Brer Deer called out, 'Brer Cooter!' A voice answered from the broomgrass, 'I'm here too!'

At every mile post, the same thing happened: Brer Deer called out, and a terrapin voice answered. By the ninth mile, Brer Deer believed he was about to tie with Brer Cooter. He ran faster, his legs pumping, his breath coming in gasps.

But at the finish line, Brer Cooter was already there, sitting on a rock, waiting.

Brer Deer collapsed from exhaustion. The terrapin had won the race and the young lady's hand. The tale reinforces that speed alone does not win — strategy, family, and preparation are just as important as raw ability.
story1199:
A classic Gullah ghost story set in the Sea Islands of Georgia. A group of women gathered for a quilting party at an old cabin on St. Helena Island. As they worked on the quilt by lantern light, they told stories to pass the night — stories of the plantation, of slavery, of the spirits that walked the island.

An old woman named Sarah, whose grandmother had been enslaved on the plantation before the Civil War, told them about the cabin's history. It was said that a young enslaved woman named Liza had died there, waiting for her husband who had been sold away. She had sat by the window every night, watching the road, waiting for him to come back. He never came. She died of a broken heart.

As Sarah finished the story, the women heard footsteps on the porch. The door creaked open, and a young woman in an old-fashioned dress stood there, looking at the quilting frame.

The women froze. The young woman was translucent — they could see the wall through her body — and her eyes had the distant, unfocused look of someone who was seeing a world that no longer existed.

She smiled sadly, touched the quilt, and vanished.

After that night, the women always left a piece of blue fabric — haint blue — in the quilt pattern to protect the cabin. The story reflects the Gullah belief that ghosts are often not malevolent but are ancestral presences who remain connected to the places and activities they loved in life.
story1200:
Brer Wolf, determined to catch and eat Brer Rabbit, devised a plan to trap him in his own home. He studied Brer Rabbit's habits — the way he came home at dusk, the way he checked for tracks before entering, the way he listened at the door — and he found a way around them.

Brer Wolf hid in Brer Rabbit's house, behind the bed, in the dark corner where the shadows were deepest. He planned to spring out when Brer Rabbit returned, catching him off guard, before he could run or think or trick his way out.

But Brer Rabbit, always cautious, noticed fresh tracks around the door and realized something was wrong. The tracks were too large for a rabbit, too deep for a possum, and too deliberate for a stray dog. Something was in his house.

He called out, pretending to talk to himself: 'I wonder if Brer Wolf is in there. I'll just go ask my friend the cow if there's any fresh wolf tracks around.'

Brer Wolf, thinking quickly, tied a string to a rock that he bounced to make it sound like he was not there. But Brer Rabbit saw through the trick.

"If Brer Wolf is in there," Brer Rabbit said, "I'll burn him out." He set the house on fire.

Brer Wolf burned to death inside, or in other versions, escaped with his fur singed and vowed revenge.

The story shows that Brer Rabbit's caution and intelligence allow him not just to escape but to turn the predator's own trap against him. Among African American audiences, the tale resonated as a message to the powerless: vigilance and cleverness can defeat even the most determined enemy.
story1201:
Brer Bear, hungry and irritable, decided he would catch the enormous bullfrog that kept him awake at night with its croaking. The frog sat at the edge of the pond, its throat pulsing with each croak, its eyes half-closed in what Brer Bear interpreted as mockery.

He found the frog at the pond's edge and made a grab, but the frog leaped into the water. Brer Bear decided to drink the entire pond dry.

He drank until his belly was swollen, but the pond level barely sank. Then the bullfrog surfaced and teased him, telling him that he would never succeed.

Brer Bear, in a rage, plunged his head underwater to catch the frog by force, but only got his head stuck in the mud. He thrashed and struggled, but the mud held him fast, and his enormous rump stuck up from the pond like a bizarre monument.

Brer Rabbit and Brer Fox passed by and laughed at the sight. They pulled him out, but Brer Bear was so embarrassed that he retreated into the deep woods and never bothered the bullfrog again.

The bullfrog is still there, croaking triumphantly. The tale illustrates that brute force and rage are futile against nature's defenses, and that the bully often ends up humiliated by those he sought to dominate.
story1202:
Brer Possum once had the most beautiful, bushy tail in the animal kingdom. It was thick and soft, with fur that gleamed like silk, and Brer Possum was so proud of it that he spent all his time grooming and displaying it, neglecting to gather food for the winter.

When winter came, Brer Possum was starving. He went to Brer Rabbit and begged for food. Brer Rabbit, always the trickster, offered him a deal: if Brer Possum would let Brer Rabbit cut off his beautiful tail, Brer Rabbit would give him food for the entire winter.

Brer Possum refused at first. His tail was his pride, his identity, the thing that made him special. But as hunger grew, as the cold bit and his belly ached, he reluctantly agreed.

Brer Rabbit cut off the bushy tail and gave Brer Possum food. But the tail never grew back, and only a thin, hairless, rat-like tail remained. Brer Possum was so ashamed that he learned to play dead whenever anyone looked at him, so they wouldn't see his shameful tail.

To this day, possums have hairless tails and play dead when frightened, eternally reminded of the price of vanity.
story1203:
An African American origin tale explaining skin color, collected by Joel Chandler Harris. According to Uncle Remus, in the beginning, all people were the same color. The Lord was making people and set them out to bake in the sun, like bread. He planned to bake them different shades — some light, some dark, some in between.

The first batch was put in the oven, but the Lord became busy with other matters and left them too long. When he took them out, they were burnt quite black. That was the Negro.

The second batch, watched more carefully, came out just right — a nice golden brown. That was the Indian.

The third batch, watched too nervously, was pulled out too soon and came out pale and undercooked. That was the white man.

The story is told with characteristic humor and is typical of African American 'why' tales that use wit to explain natural phenomena, often with a subtle commentary on racial hierarchy. While using self-deprecating humor, the tale subtly subverts racist ideologies by suggesting racial difference is mere accident of timing in the divine kitchen.
